steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper that introduces a large-scale benchmark for learning from label proportions (LLP) on tabular data. Explain what LLP is and why it matters for privacy, why tabular data lacks a good benchmark, what feature bags are, and summarize our contributions and the choice of base datasets.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Supervised learning vs learning from label proportions (LLP)
- Why LLP matters now: privacy and applications
- Image vs tabular LLP evaluation; no large-scale tabular benchmark
- Feature bags in tabular LLP
- Contributions: LLP-Bench datasets, hardness metrics, large evaluation
- Choice of base datasets (Criteo CTR and SSCL); classification and regression settings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Supervised learning vs LLP
  - supervised: feature-vectors (instances) + labels; model predicts labels of test instances
  - privacy concerns, rarity of high-quality large-scale supervised data -> LLP gained importance (cite)
  - LLP: training data aggregated into bags; each bag = instances + aggregated label count; goal: instance-level classifier (cite)
- Why LLP matters
  - privacy landscape: restrictions on tracking user events -> LLP formulation of user-modeling in online advertising (cite)
  - only average label per bag revealed; bag size = measure of privacy
  - other applications: medical records anonymization, IVF prediction, image classification, mass spectrometry, legal constraints, inadequate/costly supervision (cite each)
- Image vs tabular
  - evaluated on image (cite) and tabular (cite) datasets
  - images: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST, random partition into bags -> medium-large LLP datasets
  - tabular: independent rows of feature vectors, one more labels each
  - previous works: small UCI-derived datasets (cite) -> no diversity or scale
  - tabular data common: online advertising, health care, scientific simulation (cite each)
  - very large data from online user interaction (cite) or user studies (cite)
  - privacy leaks matter more at large scale -> LLP on large tabular data critical
  - image LLP has CIFAR-* benchmarks; nothing equivalent for tabular
- Feature bags
  - unique to tabular LLP (cite)
  - all instances in a bag share value of grouping key(s)
  - real use: online advertising, conversion labels aggregated over pre-selected categorical features (cite)
  - Figure 1: three datasets from same instances; first random (like CIFAR-*, cite); second and third feature bags with F1, F2 and F3 as grouping keys
  - feature bags can also be fixed size
- Contributions (LLP-Bench)
  - 56 LLP datasets (52 feature bag, 4 random bag) from Criteo CTR, 45 million instances (cite)
  - 14 LLP datasets (10 feature bag, 4 random bag) from Criteo SSCL, TBA million instances (cite)
  - diverse bag construction; feature bag datasets remove bags of extreme sizes; 13.5 million to 24.75 million bags
  - first large-scale tabular LLP benchmark (Section 4)
  - four metrics for hardness of an LLP dataset; analysis of the 56 datasets (Sections 3, 5)
  - 9 SOTA/popular tabular LLP techniques on all 56 Criteo CTR datasets; 3 of them on the 14 SSCL datasets (regression); more than 3000 experiments (Sections 6, 7)
- Choice of base datasets
  - impression-click and click-conversion -> natural LLP aggregation from user privacy (cite)
  - few public large-scale tabular datasets with many categorical features -> rich feature bags
  - techniques more general, but restricted to these: binary \{0,1\} click labels, or number of conversions per click
  - binary setting widely studied; LLP applications in IVF prediction and high-energy physics (cite x2)
  - regression: remote sensing, real-valued labels only as aggregates (cite)
  - user-modeling in online advertising -> LLP formulation (see Section 1 of cite), classification or regression

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the usual supervised learning setting, the training data is made of feature-vectors (instances) together with their labels. A model is trained on such data and then used at inference time to predict the labels of test instances. Recently, mostly because of privacy concerns and because high quality large-scale supervised data is relatively rare, the weakly supervised framework of learning from label proportions (LLP) has become important. In LLP, the training data is aggregated into bags. Each bag has a bunch of instances (and their feature vectors) and the aggregated label count for them. The goal is to learn a classification model that predicts the class-labels of the individual instances.

LLP has recently become important to study because of changes in the privacy landscape. In particular, restrictions on tracking user events have led to an LLP formulation of user-modeling in online advertising. Since only the average label of a bag of users is revealed, the size of the bags measures how much privacy is afforded. There are other applications too, like medical records anonymization, IVF prediction, image classification, mass spectrometry, datasets with legal constraints and inadequate or costly supervision.

These LLP techniques have mainly been evaluated and studied on image and tabular datasets. For images, well known datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST are used to create medium-large scale LLP datasets, usually by randomly partitioning the dataset into bags. Tabular data, on the other hand, consists of independent rows of feature vectors with one more labels attached to each feature vector. Previous works often used tabular LLP datasets derived from small UCI datasets, and these do not simulate the diversity and scale of applications that involve such data. Tabular datasets are actually extremely common in real world classification and regression tasks, for online advertising, health care research and scientific simulation studies. These applications usually use very large scale data, either from online user interaction or user studies. If sensitive data is exposed by accident, the impact of the privacy leak is much higher in large scale datasets. So LLP on large scale tabular datasets is a very critical application and the research community is paying more and more attention to it. Image LLP has large scale benchmark datasets derived from CIFAR-*, but there is no equivalent benchmark for tabular data.

Recent literature points out a unique property of tabular LLP, which is the notion of feature bags. With feature bags, the bags are constructed so that all instances in a bag have the same value for given key(s), called the grouping key(s). These bags occur in critical real-world applications like user modelling in online advertising, where the conversion labels are aggregated over pre-selected categorical features. Figure 1 shows three datasets created from the same instance datasets. The first dataset is created by random sampling, much like the ones created from CIFAR-*. The second and third datasets are feature bags created by using F1, F2 and F3 as the grouping keys respectively. Feature bags can also be made to have fixed size.

- motivated by this: LLP-Bench, large scale diverse benchmark for tabular LLP; three contributions
  1. LLP-Bench suite:
     - 56 LLP datasets (52 feature bag, 4 random bag) from Criteo CTR prediction dataset, 45 million instances
     - 14 LLP datasets (10 feature bag, 4 random bag) from Criteo SSCL, TBA million instances
     - diverse bag construction; feature bag datasets drop extreme-size bags; 13.5 million to 24.75 million bags; first such benchmark (Section 4)
  2. four metrics for hardness of an LLP dataset; analysis of the 56 datasets (Sections 3, 5)
  3. 9 SOTA/popular tabular LLP techniques on all 56 CTR datasets; 3 on the 14 SSCL datasets (regression); more than 3000 experiments (Sections 6, 7)
- choice of base datasets: impression-click / click-conversion -> LLP from user privacy; few public large tabular datasets with many categorical features; binary \{0,1\} click labels or number of conversions per click
- binary setting widely studied (IVF prediction, high-energy physics); regression in remote sensing; user-modeling in online advertising -> LLP formulation, classification or regression

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the usual supervised learning setting, the training data is made of feature-vectors (instances) together with their labels. A model is trained on such data and then used at inference time to predict the labels of test instances. Recently, mostly because of privacy concerns and because high quality large-scale supervised data is relatively rare, the weakly supervised framework of learning from label proportions (LLP) has become important. In LLP, the training data is aggregated into bags. Each bag has a bunch of instances (and their feature vectors) and the aggregated label count for them. The goal is to learn a classification model that predicts the class-labels of the individual instances.

LLP has recently become important to study because of changes in the privacy landscape. In particular, restrictions on tracking user events have led to an LLP formulation of user-modeling in online advertising. Since only the average label of a bag of users is revealed, the size of the bags measures how much privacy is afforded. There are other applications too, like medical records anonymization, IVF prediction, image classification, mass spectrometry, datasets with legal constraints and inadequate or costly supervision.

These LLP techniques have mainly been evaluated and studied on image and tabular datasets. For images, well known datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST are used to create medium-large scale LLP datasets, usually by randomly partitioning the dataset into bags. Tabular data, on the other hand, consists of independent rows of feature vectors with one more labels attached to each feature vector. Previous works often used tabular LLP datasets derived from small UCI datasets, and these do not simulate the diversity and scale of applications that involve such data. Tabular datasets are actually extremely common in real world classification and regression tasks, for online advertising, health care research and scientific simulation studies. These applications usually use very large scale data, either from online user interaction or user studies. If sensitive data is exposed by accident, the impact of the privacy leak is much higher in large scale datasets. So LLP on large scale tabular datasets is a very critical application and the research community is paying more and more attention to it. Image LLP has large scale benchmark datasets derived from CIFAR-*, but there is no equivalent benchmark for tabular data.

Recent literature points out a unique property of tabular LLP, which is the notion of feature bags. With feature bags, the bags are constructed so that all instances in a bag have the same value for given key(s), called the grouping key(s). These bags occur in critical real-world applications like user modelling in online advertising, where the conversion labels are aggregated over pre-selected categorical features. Figure 1 shows three datasets created from the same instance datasets. The first dataset is created by random sampling, much like the ones created from CIFAR-*. The second and third datasets are feature bags created by using F1, F2 and F3 as the grouping keys respectively. Feature bags can also be made to have fixed size.

Because of these observations and the richness of the problem, we propose LLP-Bench, a large scale, diverse benchmark for tabular LLP. This paper makes three contributions, listed below.

1. We propose LLP-Bench, a suite of

- 56 LLP datasets (52 feature bag and 4 random bag datasets) created from the popular Criteo CTR prediction dataset, which has 45 million instances.

- 14 LLP datasets (10 feature bag and 4 random bag datasets) created from the more recently available Criteo Sponsored Search Conversion Logs (Criteo SSCL), which has TBA million instances.

These LLP datasets represent diverse ways of constructing bags from the underlying tabular data. The feature bag datasets involve removing bags of extreme sizes, and they contain 13.5 million to 24.75 million bags. As far as we know, LLP-Bench is the first large scale tabular LLP benchmark with this much diversity in the datasets it contains (Section 4).

2. We propose four metrics that help to characterize and quantify how hard an LLP dataset is. Using these four metrics we give a deep analysis of the 56 datasets in LLP-Bench (Sections 3, 5).

3. We present the performance of 9 SOTA and popular tabular LLP techniques on all the 56 datasets of LLP-Bench that come from the Criteo CTR prediction dataset. Some of these techniques can't be applied to regression datasets, so we evaluate 3 of them on the 14 LLP-Bench datasets that correspond to Criteo Sponsored Search Conversion Logs. As far as we know, our study has more than 3000 experiments and is the most extensive evaluation of popular tabular LLP techniques in the literature (Sections 6, 7).

Choice of base datasets. The Criteo CTR and SSCL datasets are relevant to our work. First, they are impression-click and click-conversion datasets, which correspond to natural applications where LLP aggregation can happen because of user privacy. Another reason is that they are among the few large scale tabular datasets that are publicly available and have several categorical features, which allows a rich collection of feature bag datasets. Our techniques for feature-based grouping and for LLP dataset analysis can be applied more generally. But since we focus on a tabular LLP Benchmark, we restrict ourselves to these datasets, in which either the feature-vectors represent impressions and get binary \{0,1\} -labels that indicate a click, or they represent clicks and the label is the number of conversions for that click.

The binary label setting is widely studied in supervised machine learning, and also in the LLP setting, with many real-world applications: see for example earlier work for applications in IVF prediction and high-energy physics. On the other hand there are regression applications in remote sensing where the real-valued labels are only available as aggregates. In particular, the important task of user-modeling on online advertising platforms has recently had privacy related restrictions that lead to an LLP formulation for it (see Section 1 of earlier work), and this is usually a classification or a regression problem.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In traditional supervised learning, training data consists of feature-vectors (instances) along with their labels. A model trained on such data is then used during inference to predict the labels of test instances. Recently, primarily due to privacy concerns and the relative rarity of high quality large-scale supervised data, the weakly supervised framework of learning from label proportions (LLP) has gained importance [1,2,3,4] In LLP, the training data is aggregated into bags. Each bag contains a bunch of instances (and their feature vectors) and their corresponding aggregated label count. The goal is to learn a classification model for predicting the class-labels of individual instances [5,6].

The study of LLP has recently gained importance due to developments in the privacy landscape. In particular, restrictions on tracking of user events have led to an LLP formulation of user-modeling in online advertising [7]. Since only the average label for a bag of users is revealed, the size of the bags is a measure of the privacy afforded. Other applications include medical records anonymization [4], IVF prediction [8], image classification [9,10], mass spectrometry [11], datasets with legal constraints [3,4] and inadequate or costly supervision [12,11].

Such LLP techniques have primarily been evaluated and studied on image [13,14,15,16,17,18] and tabular [2,19,20] datasets. On images, well known datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, MNIST are used – typically by randomly partitioning the dataset into bags – to create medium-large scale LLP datasets. Tabular data, on the other hand, consists of independent rows of feature vectors with one more labels attached to each feature vector. Previous works often used tabular LLP datasets derived from small UCI [21] datasets, which fail to simulate the diversity and scale of applications involving such data. Notably, tabular datasets are extremely common in real world classification and regression tasks for online advertising [7], health care research [3,4] and scientific simulation studies [11]. Such applications tend to use very large scale data either from online user interaction [22,23] or user studies [24]. The impact of privacy leaks due to inadvertent exposure of sensitive data is much higher in large scale datasets. Therefore LLP on large scale tabular datasets is a very critical application that is receiving increasing attention from the research community. While image LLP has large scale benchmark datasets derived from CIFAR-*, no equivalent benchmark exists for tabular data.

A unique property of tabular LLP, as pointed out in recent literature [2,25], is the notion of feature bags. In feature bags, bags are constructed such that all instances within a bag have the same value for given key(s) called the grouping key(s). Such bags occur in critical real-world applications such as user modelling in online advertising, where the conversion labels are aggregated over pre-selected categorical features [25,19,7]. Figure 1 shows three datasets created from the same instance datasets. The first dataset is created by random sampling, much like the ones created using CIFAR-* [13,14,15]. The second and third datasets are feature bags created by using F1, F2 and F3 as the grouping keys respectively. Note that feature bags can also be made to have fixed size.

Motivated by the above observations and the richness of the problem, we propose LLP-Bench, a large scale, diverse benchmark for tabular LLP. We make three contributions in this paper, listed below.

1. We propose LLP-Bench, a suite of

- 56 LLP datasets (52 feature bag and 4 random bag datasets) created from the popular Criteo CTR prediction dataset consisting of 45 million instances [26].

- 14 LLP datasets (10 feature bag and 4 random bag datasets) created from the more recently available Criteo Sponsored Search Conversion Logs (Criteo SSCL) containing TBA million instances [27].

These LLP datasets represent diverse ways in which bags can be constructed from underlying tabular data. The feature bag datasets entail removing bags of extreme sizes, and contain 13.5 million to 24.75 million bags (this should be instances, change numbers also). To the best of our knowledge, LLP-Bench is the first large scale tabular LLP benchmark with such extensive diversity in its constituent datasets (Section 4).

2. We propose four metrics that help characterize and quantify the hardness of an LLP dataset. Using these four metrics we present a deep analysis of the 56 datasets in LLP-Bench (Sections 3, 5).

3. We present the performance of 9 SOTA and popular tabular LLP techniques on all the 56 datasets of LLP-Bench derived from the Criteo CTR prediction dataset. Some of these techniques are not applicable to regression datasets, so we evaluate 3 of them on the 14 datasets of LLP-Bench corresponding to Criteo Sponsored Search Conversion Logs. To the best of our knowledge, our study, consisting of more than 3000 experiments, is the most extensive evaluation of popular tabular LLP techniques in the literature (Sections 6, 7).

Choice of base datasets. The Criteo CTR and SSCL datasets are relevant to our work. Firstly, they are impression-click and click-conversion datasets, which correspond to natural applications where LLP aggregation can occur due to user privacy [7]. Another reason is that they are among the few publicly available large scale tabular datasets with several categorical features, which allow for a rich collection of feature bag datasets. Our techniques for feature-based grouping and LLP dataset analysis are more generally applicable. However, since we focus on a tabular LLP Benchmark, we restrict ourselves to these datasets, in which either the feature-vectors represent impressions and are given binary \{0,1\} -labels indicating a click, or they represent clicks and the label indicates the number of conversions for that click.

The binary label setting is widely studied in supervised machine learning, and in the LLP setting as well, with many real-world applications: see e.g. references [8] and [12] in the paper for applications in IVF prediction and high-energy physics. On the other hand, there are regression applications in remote sensing [28,29] in which the real-valued labels are available only as aggregates. In particular, the important task of user-modeling on online advertising platforms has recently seen privacy related restrictions leading to an LLP formulation for it (see Section 1 of [19]), which is typically a classification or a regression problem.
